messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Evelyn, a 78‑year‑old graphic designer who still hovers over a computer screen in the small studio she and her husband share, recalls the night the storm rolled through the coastal town of her youth. The wind howled like a living thing, tearing windows and bending the familiar brick houses into shapes that had never existed before. She was in bed when the first sheets of rain hit the roof, but it was the sudden, deafening roar of the wind that pushed the front door wide open, shattering the fragile calm she had cultivated for years. The memory of that moment is not a single, vivid episode; it is a collage of sensations that feels as if it is happening now, a present‑ticking echo that refuses to leave her mind. She can recall the metallic taste of fear, yet her body feels numb, as though the event had happened to a stranger. The sound of a door slamming, the sight of a broken window, the scent of spilled wine after a neighbor’s party—all have become auditory, visual, and olfactory triggers that yank her back into that night. When she hears a door click in her own home, she feels a rush of dread and immediately begins to think of loss, of loved ones she could have protected. These triggers lead her to shatter her previously stable beliefs about safety and order; she has come to believe the world is a dangerous place where injustice rules. The belief that the storm was utterly unfair, that no one could prevent it, fuels the sense that her life has been violently uprooted. This sense of injustice feeds directly into her negative appraisals, and those appraisals in turn reinforce the triggers that haunt her. Evelyn’s negative appraisal of a dangerous, unfair world pushes her toward maladaptive strategies. She spends hours staring at her desk, counting the lines of a still‑unfinished poster, repeatedly re‑arranging the layout of her tools to feel in control. The compulsive cleaning—she is certain that if she keeps everything perfect, she can ward off another catastrophe—becomes an anchor for her day. She also engages in prevention rumination, constantly replaying how different decisions might have altered the storm’s impact. These rumination sessions deepen her memory of the event, especially the feeling that the story is unreal—she cannot accept that the house, once safe, could have been torn asunder. The more she thinks of the “what ifs,” the more she feels the memory’s emotional numbness intensify, and her body responds by tightening her fingers around the paintbrush. The memory of the night, in turn, fuels her maladaptive strategies. Each time she remembers the door’s sudden opening, she feels compelled to lock every door and window in her home, to check twice, to wash her hands until the water is clear, as if cleaning can erase a trauma. This compulsive cleaning creates a feedback loop: by spending hours in a state of over‑control, she only reinforces the feeling that she is constantly on guard, and her sense of a dangerous world grows more entrenched. The memory’s unreal quality—she cannot believe it happened to her—pushes her to attempt erasing it, to forget it by focusing on bright colors and client briefs, yet the act of memory erasure itself feeds back into the memory, making it more vivid each time she tries to suppress it. The triggers, negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and memory weave together into a self‑reinforcing pattern that has dominated her days. She avoids walking down the street at dusk, the last hours of the day when the wind begins to pick up, fearing a sudden gust might crack another window. She even postpones her weekly client calls, telling herself that the thought of a door shutting on her during the conversation would be unbearable. These avoidance behaviors create tangible consequences: her husband has had to take over more responsibilities, and a few of her recent design projects have stalled because she is too anxious to focus. Her sense of shattered beliefs, that the world is an unpredictable and unjust place, now colours every interaction she has, turning even familiar tasks into potential catastrophes. It was the night she finally sat down to finish a brochure for a local charity, when a sudden slam of a door in the hallway made her heart leap so violently she almost lost her composure. She realized that if she could no longer work at her own pace, if her life was controlled by these invisible hands of fear, she needed help. Evelyn’s most pressing fear is that she will never reclaim the sense of control she once had, that her creative mind will remain hostage to the night’s echo. Yet she also holds a fragile hope that with the right support she might learn to separate the storm’s roar from her everyday life, to let the door open without it tearing her world apart.
